Press Release:


Marabastad: Asylum Seekers’ Nightmare
Getting refugee status from the Marabastad Department of Home Affairs should mark the start of a new life for asylum seekers, who flock to South Africa from as far afield as Syria. But, claims by Home Affairs that the registration process has been streamlined are in stark contrast to applicants’ experiences of a journey fraught with bribery, corruption and abuse. Carte Blanche investigates.




Script:


The sun’s rays warm hundreds of souls waiting in line at the only home affairs office processing asylum seeker applications. Located in Pretoria, last year over 200 000 applicants were dealt with here.
B LINK: “This is the Marabastad home affairs office where refugees and asylum seekers are processed, it’s a little after 7 in the morning and many of these people have been here since the morning hours, but there is no guarantee they will be attended to today.”
The applicants hope to be granted refugee status. This would allow them to work, study, apply for a bank account and a cell phone. Without this status they remain undocumented and live in limbo.
Mayihlome “The refugee act is trying to protect those who have a well founded fear of persecution in their country.”
Home Affairs Deputy Director General of Communications Mayihlome Tshwete says it’s up to the officials at Marabastad to hear an asylum seeker’s story, and decide if it’s reasonably true and if it aligns with the legal definition of a refugee.
Mayihlome “If we have 100 applicants, we expect 90 of them to be economic migrants who are just looking for work opportunities.”
The department of Home Affairs has prioritized the provision of more work permits to economic migrants to unclog the system.
B LINK: “It’s an extraordinary thing to say, but in a way these are the lucky ones, because an estimated 60% of all refugees do not survive the journey to South Africa. But after all their hardships this is not the end of the road, because in a sense, their troubles are just beginning.”
According to reports what foreigners in fact wait in line for, is the approach of corruption. This was confirmed when we visited.
Interpreter: “Baba, I take you in, anything you didn’t do here, your picture here, your finger print, me and you will be here until you get your paper.
Maher Haikal and his wife Angie Madani grew up and fell in love in Syria. They thought they’d spend the rest of their lives there.
Maher “It was amazing, I used to study at two colleges, I used to do sports and join clubs, it was a nice a life.”
In March 2011, Syria erupted in a bloody civil war - Maher’s house was completely destroyed and his uncle was kidnapped.
Angie: “We had no jobs anymore, there is no life, every time you walk down the street you find a missile going down.”
The couple decided to leave – but would they make the dangerous boat journey to Europe – like Angie’s brother had?
Angie: “You pay a fortune and pay a person who is not trusted, in a very small boat in the ocean.”
OR would they start life elsewhere?
Maher: “I was only looking at South Africa – from 2010 – the football, and we saw mandela and everyone is free.”
They managed to obtain visas to South Africa. Arriving in February last year seeking refugee status, they went to Marabastad.
Angie “We’ve been asked for bribes, and money for every single task, they ask you for money.”
Bongani: “ Who asks you for money?
Angie: “The employees, the interpreters, even the security, every single person there. Every time we go there, to get into the building you have to pay the security just to get inside the building.”
The couple forks out about R1000 each time they go to Marabastad.
Maher: we’ve been here for a year and half… humiliation.”
Angie “We’re asylum seekers and they are not supposed to be paying anything. And I hate having to do this because I know it’s wrong, we’re forced to do it, because there is no other way to get your paper done.”
Only Angie had an interview, as Maher’s file was lost.
Angie: “Then one of the inspectors asked him for 500 to find the file.”
Then strangely Angie’s asylum application was rejected and Maher’s granted.
Angie “It said Damascus is safe.”
Bongani: “Your husband got an approval and you did not?
Angie: No, and we’re family.
When Angie asked why, she was devastated by the official’s answer.
Angie: “This is not Syria, this is South Africa, if you don’t like how we operate, if you don’t like it just go back and die in Syria.”
“Gabriel,” is from West Africa. Like Angie and Maher, he fears for his life. He says he was hunted by Boko Haram soldiers for having different religious beliefs. After they kidnapped and murdered his family, he fled on foot.
Gabriel: “What’s the point of being alive actually. If this is real, God just kill me.”
Traumatized he was smuggled without documents into South Africa where he slept on Pretoria’s streets until he met “Rachel” at a church. She sympathized with his struggles.
Rachel “He just touches people’s hearts. You know what, he’s got a lot of love.”
Rachel decided to help Gabriel with his asylum application.
Gabriel “The first time I went to Marabastad I remember I saw a very long line there.”
Bongani: What was the process?
Gabriel: “A guy came and said come I’ll take you inside for R700.”
Rachel: “They don’t even have money for food, and but they have to go and pay all the bribery money.”
Gabriel queued for over a year – he was beaten and robbed in the que, finally after paying more than R10,000 he managed to enter the building.
Gabriel: “Just to get my interview I had to pay R2,000. People will say guy, just comply, you’re a foreigner, if they say just pay, just pay, whom will you get help from anyway.”
He says the woman who interviewed him did not capture his story accurately. When he complained, she refused to fix it. He was then issued with a “Fraudulent decision” finding, so he had to enter the appeals process to have it set aside and go for a second interview.
Gabriel: “It seems like this woman’s version verging together with what happened to me, to create another version which I have to go and defend at the appeal board now.”
Bongani: “Is the Asylum system in south Africa working?”
Wayne: “The simple answer is no, a lot of asylum seekers and refugee’s do not have access to the services in the asylum system.”
Wayne Ncube works for Lawyers for Human rights – an NGO that offers pro-bono assistance.
Wayne ” We’ve have clients who have been waiting 12 years… last year there were no positive decisions that came out of our Masena refugee offices. This was down from 40 percent the previous year.
Mayi “The inefficiency’s and the challenges that we face at marabastad have worked very well for a certain group of people, home affairs officials, security officials, but also those who want to get into the country and see it as the easiest way to get into the country.”
Mayihlome says they introduced a box system for applicants to deposit their documents directly, eliminating the personal contact which often leads to corruption. The stamped documents are handed back with a decision or date on which to return for the next step. Yet, Wayne says the majority of successful cases are still only a result of going all the way to the appeals process - and currently even this is not working.
Wayne: “At the refugee appeal board, they are not even hearing matters because they don’t have a chairman right now.”
Angie: “Many times people lost their papers, I saw people put their papers in the box and then they don’t get them back and they are forced to pay a bribe – that happened to us once.”
Bognani: “So if that’s your only copy, you’re finished.”
Angie: “Yes, you’ve got no papers anymore.”
Mayihlome calls on the public to report corruption. We visited the notorious Marabastad office with hidden cameras to find out for ourselves. This man claimed to be an interpreter and was seen inside the building assisting applicants.
Interpreter: “Stay with me and just like a brother, I take you in and get you everything. I told you guys 500, or don’t come back, nobody can do it for you for 400. I’ve been at this office for 9 years, you can ask anybody.”
Mayihlome “We are completely disgusted as department by people who take advantage of people who are seeking services.”
We confronted him to ask why he was taking bribes to provide a service that’s free.
Bongani : “I’m from Carte Blanche we wanted to ask…”
B LINK: “We really wanted to know why he has taken advantage of these very desperate and vulnerable people, but he’s got no answers for us.”
We then met a man driving a police car who identified himself as an undercover police officer called “Silver” because of his silver teeth. Silver said the R1,500 he charges is not exchanged inside the building.
Silver “I got and give somebody straight and they’ll organize form, they’ll write for you don’t write. Until finger print and snap (picture).
Mayi: “Now we’ve introduced a system where within a space of an hour, the department comes in an tells them how many people they are going to serve on that day, its made it very difficult for these guys to operate, so they come in the morning, and they lie to people and try to get them into the system.”
For R500 more his connections will make up a suitable story for you.
Silver “If you talk about Boko Haram, immediately talk about it, Google and check with the phone which year and which month and who was causin the problem there-the head. You know to buy a statement from the interpreter is 500Rands.”
Home Affairs kicked into action. Investigators from Bvisa Masina – a ministerial operation to catch dirty government officials – set a trap with the help of the police’s directorate for priority crime investigations unit. Counter corruption investigator Nokthula Similane explains the undercover operation.”
NS: “As part of the entrapment, some of the affidavits that were utilized were bogus affidavits that were compiled by SAPS.”
Their goal? To catch syndicate members like the interpreter or Silver red handed. On day one the agents were approached by the interpreter and they paid him.
NS: “However, the documents as promised were not received by the agent.”
It’s likely our interpreter has connections inside and has access to the department’s printers, but the investigation will continue and they promise to keep us updated.
Interpreter: “Others may print the documents but they are not in the system. Be careful.”
As for Silver…
Silver: “If I charge you R1500, I know I’ll pay everything.”
He approached the undercover agents too, and tried his luck, but this confident trickster didn’t follow through. The SAPS has not yet verified that he is in fact a police officer. But the vehicle WAS confirmed to be that of the SAPS.
So we called to ask him for an interview on the number he gave us when we met him undercover. The man on the phone initially confirmed he was officer Silver, but then quickly changed his tune.
Silver: “No, it’s Ronald, and I’m in Cape Town right now.”
Journalist: “Okay I believe this is the number of a police officer.”
Hangs up.
On day two of the operation, the police’s agents were approached by a THIRD man ALSO claiming to be an interpreter. He produced fraudulent documents and although we couldn’t film the covert operation, the department made an arrest.
NAT SOUND
This man was found with the money marked and used to ensnare him, a police reservist badge, two bullets and – the mega load– a stack of asylum documents!
Their authenticity hasn’t yet been confirmed but Nokthula says he is not an interpreter employed by the department.
Nokthula: “He could possibly charged with the following contravention of the legistlations, namely corruption, immigration act and the refugee act.”
The investigations will continue. But the burning question remains: why is Marabastad the only facility taking asylum applications? Lawyers for Human Rights have obtained several court orders saying the department must re-open other branches.
Mayi “There is an ongoing attempt by the department to move these processing centres to points of entry, it’s not to close them down indefinitely. So now the applicant is not more exposed to exploitation.”
Ultimately, Home Affairs wants to determine a refugee’s status immediately and capture all information digitally. Meanwhile, Gabriel is healing from his trauma.
Gabriel “Everyone I cared about are dead anyway, but you find new people come into your life and you start caring about them, because of these people you actually want to get through it.”
Maher and Angie remain hopeful.
Bongani: “For better or worse hey?”
Angie: “Yes (smiles).”
They love this country, but want to be treated like human beings.

Mayi: “Now we’ve introduced a system where within a space of an hour, the department comes in an tells them how many people they are going to serve on that day, its made it very difficult for these guys to operate, so they come in the morning, and they lie to people and try to get them into the system.” For R500 more his connections will make up a suitable story for you. Silver “If you talk about Boko Haram, immediately talk about it, Google and check with the phone which year and which month and who was causin the problem there-the head. You know to buy a statement from the interpreter is 500Rands.” Home Affairs kicked into action. Investigators from Bvisa Masina – a ministerial operation to catch dirty government officials – set a trap with the help of the police’s directorate for priority crime investigations unit. Counter corruption investigator Nokthula Similane explains the undercover operation.” NS: “As part of the entrapment, some of the affidavits that were utilized were bogus affidavits that were compiled by SAPS.” Their goal? To catch syndicate members like the interpreter or Silver red handed. On day one the agents were approached by the interpreter and they paid him. NS: “However, the documents as promised were not received by the agent.” It’s likely our interpreter has connections inside and has access to the department’s printers, but the investigation will continue and they promise to keep us updated. Interpreter: “Others may print the documents but they are not in the system. Be careful.” As for Silver… Silver: “If I charge you R1500, I know I’ll pay everything.” He approached the undercover agents too, and tried his luck, but this confident trickster didn’t follow through. The SAPS has not yet verified that he is in fact a police officer. But the vehicle WAS confirmed to be that of the SAPS. So we called to ask him for an interview on the number he gave us when we met him undercover. The man on the phone initially confirmed he was officer Silver, but then quickly changed his tune. Silver: “No, it’s Ronald, and I’m in Cape Town right now.” Journalist: “Okay I believe this is the number of a police officer.” Hangs up. On day two of the operation, the police’s agents were approached by a THIRD man ALSO claiming to be an interpreter. He produced fraudulent documents and although we couldn’t film the covert operation, the department made an arrest. NAT SOUND This man was found with the money marked and used to ensnare him, a police reservist badge, two bullets and – the mega load– a stack of asylum documents! Their authenticity hasn’t yet been confirmed but Nokthula says he is not an interpreter employed by the department. Nokthula: “He could possibly charged with the following contravention of the legistlations, namely corruption, immigration act and the refugee act.” The investigations will continue. But the burning question remains: why is Marabastad the only facility taking asylum applications? Lawyers for Human Rights have obtained several court orders saying the department must re-open other branches. Mayi “There is an ongoing attempt by the department to move these processing centres to points of entry, it’s not to close them down indefinitely. So now the applicant is not more exposed to exploitation.” Ultimately, Home Affairs wants to determine a refugee’s status immediately and capture all information digitally. Meanwhile, Gabriel is healing from his trauma. Gabriel “Everyone I cared about are dead anyway, but you find new people come into your life and you start caring about them, because of these people you actually want to get through it.” Maher and Angie remain hopeful. Bongani: “For better or worse hey?” Angie: “Yes (smiles).” They love this country, but want to be treated like human beings.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Marabastad deals with asylum seekers in South Africa. It has a notorious reputation for corruption and abuse, but this year, the dept tried to stop this, has it worked? Carte Blanche Investigates.
metadata.Summary: We have long heard how marabastad has been plagued with corruption (bribery and beatings), then this year, the dept of home affairs introduced a system that they said would make corruption impossible. So we went there to investigate. We took a hidden camera and were approached by an agent who is a translator inside and a police officer who offered to get us asylum if we pay them. We have several strong case studies and will tell the story through them - they have both been offered bribes, and one was beaten.
